problems.title: Label each row
problems.statement_md: A cafe wants to tag every menu item with a price band: `'Premium'` for a price of 6.00 or more, `'Standard'` for 3.00 or more (but under 6.00), and `'Budget'` for anything cheaper. Return `item_id`, `name` and the band as `price_band`, ordered by `item_id`.

tables.name: menu_items
tables.description_md: One row per menu item.

hints_md: A CASE expression checks its WHEN branches from top to bottom and stops at the first one that is true.
Two items cost exactly 3.00 and 6.00. Which comparison operator keeps them in the higher band?
problems.notes_md:
**Concept:** CASE turns a value into a label, row by row.

**Shape:** one table, no grouping. Add a computed column that picks a label from the price, then sort by id.

**Syntax:** `CASE WHEN condition THEN result WHEN condition THEN result ELSE result END AS alias`.

**Watch out:** branches are tested in order, so put the most specific test first; and decide whether a boundary value belongs to the lower or the higher band before choosing `>` or `>=`.

solutions.label: Highest band first
solutions.explain_md: The first WHEN that is true wins, so the price is tested against 6.00, then 3.00, and ELSE catches everything cheaper. `>=` keeps the boundary values in the higher band.
solutions.sql:
SELECT item_id, name,
       CASE WHEN price >= 6.00 THEN 'Premium'
            WHEN price >= 3.00 THEN 'Standard'
            ELSE 'Budget'
       END AS price_band
FROM menu_items
ORDER BY item_id;

solutions.label: Lowest band first
solutions.explain_md: The same rule read from the other end: below 3.00 is Budget, below 6.00 is Standard, the rest is Premium. A price of exactly 3.00 fails `< 3.00`, so it correctly falls into Standard.
solutions.sql:
SELECT item_id, name,
       CASE WHEN price < 3.00 THEN 'Budget'
            WHEN price < 6.00 THEN 'Standard'
            ELSE 'Premium'
       END AS price_band
FROM menu_items
ORDER BY item_id;

traps.explain_md: `>` instead of `>=` pushes the two items priced exactly 6.00 and 3.00 into the band below.
traps.sql:
SELECT item_id, name,
       CASE WHEN price > 6.00 THEN 'Premium'
            WHEN price > 3.00 THEN 'Standard'
            ELSE 'Budget'
       END AS price_band
FROM menu_items
ORDER BY item_id;

traps.explain_md: Testing `price >= 3.00` first means every item of 3.00 or more stops at that branch, so 'Premium' is never produced.
traps.sql:
SELECT item_id, name,
       CASE WHEN price >= 3.00 THEN 'Standard'
            WHEN price >= 6.00 THEN 'Premium'
            ELSE 'Budget'
       END AS price_band
FROM menu_items
ORDER BY item_id;

problems.title: Count by label
problems.statement_md: A library sorts its books by length: `'Short'` for under 200 pages, `'Medium'` for 200 to 399 pages, and `'Long'` for 400 pages or more. Return each length as `length_band` with the number of books in it as `book_count`, most books first, ties by `length_band` alphabetically.

tables.name: books
tables.description_md: One row per book.

hints_md: First turn each book into a label. Then ask which clause collapses rows that share the same label.
GROUP BY works on any expression, not only on a plain column.
problems.notes_md:
**Concept:** group by a label you compute, not by a stored column.

**Shape:** build the label with CASE, group on that same label, count rows per group.

**Syntax:** GROUP BY accepts an expression, or the column of a subquery that already computes the label.

**Watch out:** grouping by the raw column gives one group per distinct value, not one per label. Also keep the CASE identical in SELECT and GROUP BY.

solutions.label: Repeat the CASE in GROUP BY
solutions.explain_md: The CASE decides the label for each book; GROUP BY uses the same expression so books with the same label are counted together.
solutions.sql:
SELECT CASE WHEN pages < 200 THEN 'Short'
            WHEN pages < 400 THEN 'Medium'
            ELSE 'Long'
       END AS length_band,
       COUNT(*) AS book_count
FROM books
GROUP BY CASE WHEN pages < 200 THEN 'Short'
              WHEN pages < 400 THEN 'Medium'
              ELSE 'Long'
         END
ORDER BY book_count DESC, length_band;

solutions.label: Label in a subquery first
solutions.explain_md: The inner query adds the label to every book; the outer query then groups by that finished column, so the CASE is written only once.
solutions.sql:
SELECT length_band, COUNT(*) AS book_count
FROM (
  SELECT CASE WHEN pages < 200 THEN 'Short'
              WHEN pages < 400 THEN 'Medium'
              ELSE 'Long'
         END AS length_band
  FROM books
) AS labelled
GROUP BY length_band
ORDER BY book_count DESC, length_band;

traps.explain_md: Grouping by `pages` makes one group per distinct page count, so the labels repeat and most counts are 1 instead of one row per band.
traps.sql:
SELECT CASE WHEN pages < 200 THEN 'Short'
            WHEN pages < 400 THEN 'Medium'
            ELSE 'Long'
       END AS length_band,
       COUNT(*) AS book_count
FROM books
GROUP BY pages
ORDER BY book_count DESC, length_band;

problems.title: Count yes and no in one row
problems.statement_md: A teacher logs attendance one row per student for a single class. Return exactly one row with two numbers: `present_count` (students marked `'present'`) and `absent_count` (students marked `'absent'`). Students marked `'late'` are not counted in either column.

tables.name: attendance
tables.description_md: One row per student for today's class. `status` is `'present'`, `'absent'` or `'late'`.

hints_md: You need two different counts from the same rows, so a WHERE filter alone cannot give both in one row.
Put a CASE inside the aggregate function so each row contributes only when it matches.
problems.notes_md:
**Concept:** conditional aggregation: an aggregate that only sees the rows you choose, one column per condition.

**Shape:** no GROUP BY; each output column is its own aggregate over the whole table with its own CASE inside.

**Syntax:** `CASE WHEN cond THEN x ELSE y END` yields one value per row; an aggregate then combines those values.

**Watch out:** COUNT counts every non-NULL value, including a 0. If the CASE returns 0 for non-matching rows, COUNT still counts them.

solutions.label: SUM of 1s and 0s
solutions.explain_md: Each row turns into 1 if it matches and 0 if not, and SUM adds them up, which is the number of matching rows.

solutions.label: COUNT of non-NULL results
solutions.explain_md: With no ELSE, non-matching rows produce NULL, and COUNT skips NULLs, so only matching rows are counted.

traps.explain_md: `ELSE 0` is a real value, not NULL, so COUNT counts every row. Both columns come out as the total number of rows (10).

problems.title: Default for missing labels
problems.statement_md: A parcel table stores a one-letter `delivery_code`: `'S'` means `'Standard'`, `'E'` means `'Express'` and `'P'` means `'Pickup point'`. Some parcels have an unknown code or no code at all. Return `parcel_id` and the service name as `service`, using `'Unknown'` for every parcel whose code is not one of the three, ordered by `parcel_id`.

tables.name: parcels
tables.description_md: One row per parcel. `delivery_code` may be NULL.

hints_md: What does CASE return when none of the WHEN branches is true and there is nothing else to fall back on?
A missing code is not equal to anything, so which part of the CASE has to deal with it?
problems.notes_md:
**Concept:** CASE with a default branch.

**Shape:** map each known code to a name, and let one final branch cover everything else, including NULL.

**Syntax:** searched form `CASE WHEN code = 'A' THEN ... ELSE ... END`; simple form `CASE code WHEN 'A' THEN ... ELSE ... END`.

**Watch out:** without ELSE, an unmatched row gets NULL, not an error and not an empty string.

solutions.label: Searched CASE with ELSE
solutions.explain_md: Each WHEN tests one code. Codes that match none of them, including NULL, reach ELSE and become 'Unknown'.
solutions.sql:
SELECT parcel_id,
       CASE WHEN delivery_code = 'S' THEN 'Standard'
            WHEN delivery_code = 'E' THEN 'Express'
            WHEN delivery_code = 'P' THEN 'Pickup point'
            ELSE 'Unknown'
       END AS service
FROM parcels
ORDER BY parcel_id;

solutions.label: Simple CASE with ELSE
solutions.explain_md: The column is named once after CASE and each WHEN supplies a value to compare it with. NULL matches no value, so it ends up in ELSE.
solutions.sql:
SELECT parcel_id,
       CASE delivery_code
            WHEN 'S' THEN 'Standard'
            WHEN 'E' THEN 'Express'
            WHEN 'P' THEN 'Pickup point'
            ELSE 'Unknown'
       END AS service
FROM parcels
ORDER BY parcel_id;

traps.explain_md: Without ELSE, parcels 4, 5 and 8 get NULL in `service` instead of 'Unknown'.
traps.sql:
SELECT parcel_id,
       CASE WHEN delivery_code = 'S' THEN 'Standard'
            WHEN delivery_code = 'E' THEN 'Express'
            WHEN delivery_code = 'P' THEN 'Pickup point'
       END AS service
FROM parcels
ORDER BY parcel_id;

problems.title: Match rows from two tables
problems.statement_md: A clinic keeps patients and appointments in separate tables. Return one row per appointment with `appt_id`, the patient's `name` and `appt_date`, earliest date first, ties by `appt_id`.

tables.name: patients
tables.description_md: One row per patient.

tables.name: appointments
tables.description_md: One row per appointment. `patient_id` points to `patients`.

hints_md: The patient's name is in one table and the appointment is in the other. Which column do both tables share?
After JOIN, which keyword says how the rows of the two tables are paired up?
problems.notes_md:
**Concept:** INNER JOIN pairs rows from two tables that share a key.

**Shape:** start from appointments, attach the matching patient row, select columns from both, sort.

**Syntax:** `FROM a JOIN b ON a.key = b.key`; prefix columns with a table alias, e.g. `a.col`.

**Watch out:** a join with no matching condition pairs every row of one table with every row of the other.

solutions.label: JOIN ... ON
solutions.explain_md: Each appointment is paired with the patient row whose `patient_id` equals its own. Appointments always have a patient here, so nothing is lost.
solutions.sql:
SELECT a.appt_id, p.name, a.appt_date
FROM appointments a
JOIN patients p ON p.patient_id = a.patient_id
ORDER BY a.appt_date, a.appt_id;

solutions.label: Start from patients
solutions.explain_md: Same pairing written from the other side; the order of the tables in an INNER JOIN does not change the rows returned.
solutions.sql:
SELECT a.appt_id, p.name, a.appt_date
FROM patients p
INNER JOIN appointments a ON a.patient_id = p.patient_id
ORDER BY a.appt_date, a.appt_id;

traps.explain_md: Listing both tables with a comma and no matching condition pairs every appointment with every patient: 25 rows instead of 5.

problems.title: Keep everyone, even without a match
problems.statement_md: A music academy wants every teacher listed with the instruments they teach, one row per lesson. A teacher with no lessons yet must still appear once, with `NULL` for the instrument. Return `name` and `instrument`, ordered by `teacher_id`, then `lesson_id`.

tables.name: teachers
tables.description_md: One row per teacher.

tables.name: lessons
tables.description_md: One row per lesson. `teacher_id` points to `teachers`.

hints_md: An ordinary JOIN keeps only rows that find a partner. Is there a join type that keeps all rows of one side?
The table whose rows must all survive goes on the left of the keyword.
problems.notes_md:
**Concept:** LEFT JOIN keeps every row of the left table; where the right table has no match, its columns are NULL.

**Shape:** teachers on the left, lessons on the right, joined on the teacher key. Sort by the left table's id so unmatched teachers sort cleanly.

**Syntax:** `FROM a LEFT JOIN b ON a.key = b.key`.

**Watch out:** swap the table order and you swap which side is protected.

solutions.label: LEFT JOIN
solutions.explain_md: Every teacher stays. Teachers with lessons repeat once per lesson; Dube has no lesson, so the instrument is NULL.
solutions.sql:
SELECT t.name, l.instrument
FROM teachers t
LEFT JOIN lessons l ON l.teacher_id = t.teacher_id
ORDER BY t.teacher_id, l.lesson_id;

solutions.label: RIGHT JOIN, tables swapped
solutions.explain_md: A RIGHT JOIN protects the right-hand table, so with teachers on the right the result is identical.
solutions.sql:
SELECT t.name, l.instrument
FROM lessons l
RIGHT JOIN teachers t ON l.teacher_id = t.teacher_id
ORDER BY t.teacher_id, l.lesson_id;

traps.explain_md: A plain JOIN only keeps teachers who have a lesson, so Dube vanishes.
traps.sql:
SELECT t.name, l.instrument
FROM teachers t
JOIN lessons l ON l.teacher_id = t.teacher_id
ORDER BY t.teacher_id, l.lesson_id;

problems.title: Who has nothing yet
problems.statement_md: A bookshop wants to email customers who have never placed an order. Return `customer_id` and `name` of every customer with no row in `orders`, ordered by `customer_id`.

tables.name: customers
tables.description_md: One row per customer.

tables.name: orders
tables.description_md: One row per order. `customer_id` points to `customers`.

hints_md: When a LEFT JOIN finds no partner, what do the right table's columns contain?
Which test checks for NULL: `= NULL` or something else?
problems.notes_md:
**Concept:** anti-join: keep rows that have no partner in another table.

**Shape:** LEFT JOIN so everyone stays, then keep only the rows where the right side came back empty.

**Syntax:** LEFT JOIN fills the right-side columns with NULL when there is no match; test for NULL with `IS NULL`.

**Watch out:** test a column of the right table that is never NULL when a match exists; and NULL is checked with `IS NULL`, never `= NULL`.

solutions.label: LEFT JOIN and IS NULL
solutions.explain_md: Customers with no order get NULL in every `orders` column. Filtering on `o.order_id IS NULL` keeps exactly those customers.
solutions.sql:
SELECT c.customer_id, c.name
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id
WHERE o.order_id IS NULL
ORDER BY c.customer_id;

solutions.label: NOT EXISTS
solutions.explain_md: For each customer, the subquery looks for any order; NOT EXISTS keeps the customer only when it finds none.
solutions.sql:
SELECT c.customer_id, c.name
FROM customers c
WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders o WHERE o.customer_id = c.customer_id)
ORDER BY c.customer_id;

traps.explain_md: `= NULL` is never true, not even for NULL, so the WHERE removes every row and the result is empty.
traps.sql:
SELECT c.customer_id, c.name
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id
WHERE o.order_id = NULL
ORDER BY c.customer_id;

traps.explain_md: Checking the left table's key for NULL is pointless: it is never NULL, so no row survives.
traps.sql:
SELECT c.customer_id, c.name
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id
WHERE c.customer_id IS NULL
ORDER BY c.customer_id;

problems.title: Totals across a join
problems.statement_md: A food-delivery app wants each customer's total spend. Return `customer_id`, `name` and `total_spent` (the sum of their order `amount`s). Customers who have not ordered must still appear, with a total of 0. Order by `total_spent` highest first, ties by `customer_id`.

tables.name: customers
tables.description_md: One row per customer.

tables.name: orders
tables.description_md: One row per order. `customer_id` points to `customers`.

hints_md: You need all customers, so which join type? And which clause turns many order rows into one row per customer?
SUM over zero rows gives NULL, not 0. Which function replaces a NULL with a value?
problems.notes_md:
**Concept:** join first, then aggregate the joined rows.

**Shape:** customers LEFT JOIN orders, group by the customer, add up the amount, then replace a missing total with 0.

**Syntax:** `COALESCE(x, fallback)` returns the fallback when x is NULL.

**Watch out:** an inner join silently drops customers with no orders, and SUM of nothing is NULL rather than 0.

solutions.label: LEFT JOIN, GROUP BY, COALESCE
solutions.explain_md: LEFT JOIN keeps customers without orders (their `amount` is NULL). SUM ignores NULLs and returns NULL when nothing is left, and COALESCE turns that NULL into 0.
solutions.sql:
SELECT c.customer_id, c.name, COALESCE(SUM(o.amount), 0) AS total_spent
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id
GROUP BY c.customer_id, c.name
ORDER BY total_spent DESC, c.customer_id;

solutions.label: Total per customer first, then join
solutions.explain_md: The subquery adds up orders per customer; the outer LEFT JOIN attaches those totals to every customer, and COALESCE fills the missing ones with 0.
solutions.sql:
SELECT c.customer_id, c.name, COALESCE(t.total, 0) AS total_spent
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN (
  SELECT customer_id, SUM(amount) AS total
  FROM orders
  GROUP BY customer_id
) AS t ON t.customer_id = c.customer_id
ORDER BY total_spent DESC, c.customer_id;

traps.explain_md: An inner join only keeps customers who have orders, so Cleo and Emil are missing.
traps.sql:
SELECT c.customer_id, c.name, COALESCE(SUM(o.amount), 0) AS total_spent
FROM customers c
JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id
GROUP BY c.customer_id, c.name
ORDER BY total_spent DESC, c.customer_id;

traps.explain_md: SUM over only NULL amounts is NULL, so Cleo and Emil show NULL instead of 0.
traps.sql:
SELECT c.customer_id, c.name, SUM(o.amount) AS total_spent
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id
GROUP BY c.customer_id, c.name
ORDER BY total_spent DESC, c.customer_id;

problems.title: Three tables in one query
problems.statement_md: An evening college stores students, courses and enrolments separately. Return one row per enrolment with `enrolment_id`, the student's `name` and the course `title`, ordered by `enrolment_id`.

tables.name: students
tables.description_md: One row per student.

tables.name: courses
tables.description_md: One row per course.

tables.name: enrolments
tables.description_md: One row per student signed up for a course. Both ids point to the other tables.

hints_md: `enrolments` is the link between the other two. Start from it and attach one table at a time.
Each JOIN gets its own ON, and each ON pairs a foreign key with the key it points to.
problems.notes_md:
**Concept:** a chain of joins; each JOIN adds one more table.

**Shape:** the middle (link) table connects the other two: link to students on the student key, link to courses on the course key.

**Syntax:** `FROM a JOIN b ON b.a_id = a.id JOIN c ON c.id = b.c_id`.

**Watch out:** match each key to the table it actually refers to. Ids such as 1, 2, 3 exist in every table, so a wrong pairing still returns rows, just wrong ones.

solutions.label: Start from the link table
solutions.explain_md: `enrolments` is joined to `students` through the student id and to `courses` through the course id, so every enrolment gets its student name and course title.
solutions.sql:
SELECT e.enrolment_id, s.name, c.title
FROM enrolments e
JOIN students s ON s.student_id = e.student_id
JOIN courses c ON c.course_id = e.course_id
ORDER BY e.enrolment_id;

solutions.label: Start from students
solutions.explain_md: Same chain, built outward from students; the rows returned are the same.
solutions.sql:
SELECT e.enrolment_id, s.name, c.title
FROM students s
JOIN enrolments e ON e.student_id = s.student_id
JOIN courses c ON c.course_id = e.course_id
ORDER BY e.enrolment_id;

traps.explain_md: The course is matched against the student's id instead of the enrolment's course id, so rows come back with the wrong course titles.
traps.sql:
SELECT e.enrolment_id, s.name, c.title
FROM enrolments e
JOIN students s ON s.student_id = e.student_id
JOIN courses c ON c.course_id = s.student_id
ORDER BY e.enrolment_id;

problems.title: Join condition in ON vs WHERE
problems.statement_md: A gym wants to know how many times each member checked in during March 2026 (from 2026-03-01 up to and including 2026-03-31). Every member must be listed, with 0 if they did not come in March. Return `member_id`, `name` and `march_checkins`, most check-ins first, ties by `member_id`.

tables.name: members
tables.description_md: One row per member.

tables.name: checkins
tables.description_md: One row per visit. `member_id` points to `members`.

hints_md: After a LEFT JOIN, a WHERE condition on the right table removes rows with NULL there too. Where else can a condition about the right table go?
To count visits and not rows, count a column from the right table instead of `*`.
problems.notes_md:
**Concept:** in an outer join, ON decides which rows pair up; WHERE then filters the finished result.

**Shape:** keep all members, but pair each only with March check-ins by putting the date test in the join condition; then group and count.

**Syntax:** `COUNT(b.id)` ignores NULLs, `COUNT(*)` does not.

**Watch out:** moving a right-table filter into WHERE quietly turns a LEFT JOIN into an inner join.

solutions.label: Date test inside ON
solutions.explain_md: The March test is part of the join condition, so members with no March check-in still get one row (with NULL check-in columns). COUNT of the check-in id counts only real visits.
solutions.sql:
SELECT m.member_id, m.name, COUNT(c.checkin_id) AS march_checkins
FROM members m
LEFT JOIN checkins c
       ON c.member_id = m.member_id
      AND c.checkin_date >= '2026-03-01'
      AND c.checkin_date < '2026-04-01'
GROUP BY m.member_id, m.name
ORDER BY march_checkins DESC, m.member_id;

solutions.label: Filter the right table first
solutions.explain_md: A subquery keeps only March visits, and the LEFT JOIN then attaches them to all members.
solutions.sql:
SELECT m.member_id, m.name, COUNT(c.checkin_id) AS march_checkins
FROM members m
LEFT JOIN (
  SELECT checkin_id, member_id
  FROM checkins
  WHERE checkin_date >= '2026-03-01' AND checkin_date < '2026-04-01'
) AS c ON c.member_id = m.member_id
GROUP BY m.member_id, m.name
ORDER BY march_checkins DESC, m.member_id;

traps.explain_md: The date test in WHERE throws away the NULL rows of members with no March visit, so Bo and Eli disappear instead of showing 0.
traps.sql:
SELECT m.member_id, m.name, COUNT(c.checkin_id) AS march_checkins
FROM members m
LEFT JOIN checkins c ON c.member_id = m.member_id
WHERE c.checkin_date >= '2026-03-01' AND c.checkin_date < '2026-04-01'
GROUP BY m.member_id, m.name
ORDER BY march_checkins DESC, m.member_id;

traps.explain_md: COUNT(*) counts the single NULL-filled row of a member with no visits, so Bo and Eli show 1 instead of 0.
traps.sql:
SELECT m.member_id, m.name, COUNT(*) AS march_checkins
FROM members m
LEFT JOIN checkins c
       ON c.member_id = m.member_id
      AND c.checkin_date >= '2026-03-01'
      AND c.checkin_date < '2026-04-01'
GROUP BY m.member_id, m.name
ORDER BY march_checkins DESC, m.member_id;

problems.title: Employee and their manager's name
problems.statement_md: A garden centre stores all staff in one table; `manager_id` holds the `employee_id` of the person's manager. Return each employee as `employee` and their manager's name as `manager`. The owner has no manager and must still appear, with `NULL` as manager. Order by the employee's `employee_id`.

tables.name: employees
tables.description_md: One row per staff member. `manager_id` is NULL for the owner.

hints_md: Both the employee and the manager are rows of the same table. How can one table be used twice in one query?
Give each copy its own alias. Which join keeps the employee whose manager is NULL?
problems.notes_md:
**Concept:** self-join: a table joined to itself, playing two roles.

**Shape:** one alias for the employee, another alias for the manager, joined where the employee's manager id equals the manager's own id.

**Syntax:** Give each use of the same table its own alias, e.g. `FROM t AS x ... t AS y`, and prefix every column with the alias you mean.

**Watch out:** an inner join drops anyone with no manager, since NULL matches nothing.

solutions.label: LEFT self-join
solutions.explain_md: The table appears twice, as `e` (employee) and `m` (manager). LEFT JOIN keeps Greta, whose `manager_id` is NULL and matches no manager row.
solutions.sql:
SELECT e.name AS employee, m.name AS manager
FROM employees e
LEFT JOIN employees m ON m.employee_id = e.manager_id
ORDER BY e.employee_id;

solutions.label: Scalar subquery
solutions.explain_md: For each employee the subquery looks up the manager's name; if there is no manager it returns NULL.
solutions.sql:
SELECT e.name AS employee,
       (SELECT m.name FROM employees m WHERE m.employee_id = e.manager_id) AS manager
FROM employees e
ORDER BY e.employee_id;

traps.explain_md: An inner self-join needs a manager row, so Greta (no manager) is missing.
traps.sql:
SELECT e.name AS employee, m.name AS manager
FROM employees e
JOIN employees m ON m.employee_id = e.manager_id
ORDER BY e.employee_id;

problems.title: Duplicate rows from a join
problems.statement_md: A bakery orders table holds one `delivery_fee` per order, and the items table holds one row per product line (`price` times `qty`). Return `order_id` and `order_total` = the sum of its item lines plus its delivery fee, with the fee counted once. Order by `order_id`.

tables.name: orders
tables.description_md: One row per order, with a single delivery fee.

tables.name: order_items
tables.description_md: One row per product line of an order.

hints_md: After joining, an order with three item lines appears three times. What happens to a fee that is added up on every one of those rows?
Either add the fee after summing the lines, or add up the lines per order before joining.
problems.notes_md:
**Concept:** a one-to-many join repeats the 'one' side's values once per matching row.

**Shape:** sum the item lines per order, and add the order-level fee exactly once.

**Syntax:** A subquery in FROM (`FROM (SELECT ...) AS s`) can pre-aggregate a table before it is joined.

**Watch out:** summing an order-level column after joining to a many-side table multiplies it by the number of lines.

solutions.label: Add the fee once, after SUM
solutions.explain_md: The fee is not summed; it is grouped on and added to the SUM of the lines, so it counts once however many lines the order has.
solutions.sql:
SELECT o.order_id, SUM(i.price * i.qty) + o.delivery_fee AS order_total
FROM orders o
JOIN order_items i ON i.order_id = o.order_id
GROUP BY o.order_id, o.delivery_fee
ORDER BY o.order_id;

solutions.label: Sum the lines in a subquery first
solutions.explain_md: The subquery reduces `order_items` to one row per order, so the join with `orders` can no longer repeat anything.
solutions.sql:
SELECT o.order_id, t.lines_total + o.delivery_fee AS order_total
FROM orders o
JOIN (
  SELECT order_id, SUM(price * qty) AS lines_total
  FROM order_items
  GROUP BY order_id
) AS t ON t.order_id = o.order_id
ORDER BY o.order_id;

traps.explain_md: Adding the fee inside the SUM adds it once per item line, so orders 1 and 3 (several lines) are overcharged.
traps.sql:
SELECT o.order_id, SUM(i.price * i.qty + o.delivery_fee) AS order_total
FROM orders o
JOIN order_items i ON i.order_id = o.order_id
GROUP BY o.order_id
ORDER BY o.order_id;
